Extract A: Organic boom sparks farm shortage
VICTORIAN shoppers are turning to organic food in their droves. Nationwide the demand
for organic produce has leapt by more than 80 percent since 2004. Organic processors
have even issued a plea for more farmers to adopt the techniques needed to meet the
demand.
A national study by New England University shows organic farm numbers have increased
by more than 5 per cent a year over the past five years. Australia has almost 12 million
hectares of certified organic farmland, the largest of any food-producing nation. Organic
farmer Jo Whitsed, of Corryong, believes customer recognition of the logos used by testing
authorities is an important factor in the growth rate.
“Demand has really taken off in the last few years,” she said.
“Consumers are learning about certified organic, and looking for the logo.
“They're concerned about the health benefits, the environment and animal welfare issues.”
Organic farming has been the norm for three generations of the Whitsed family on their
150 ha property in a lush valley on the upper reaches of the Murray River. Jo and Steve
Whitsed are continuing the family tradition.
There’s a chance too that Jo’s daughter, Tahnia, could become a fourth-generation organic
farmer, but at 7 she hasn't decided. No pesticides or chemicals are used, and cattle feed
on pasture rich in treated-waste products from within farm boundaries or on silage grown
and prepared on the farm. The family runs 160 dairy cows to produce organically certified
milk.
“The cows are milking the best they ever have,” said Jo Whitsed.
“We make up our own licks from cider vinegar, dolomite and molasses, and we certainly
don't get the vet out very often.”
There are seven organic certification groups in Australia, using standards established by
the Quarantine Inspection Service. Australian Certified Organic, with its sprouting-bud
logo, claims to certify about two-thirds of the genuine organic produce.
“Shoppers need to look for the certification logo,” said Dr Andrew Monk, of Biological
Farmers Australia. “It is harder to farm organically and the product will cost more.
“Consumers make a conscious decision to choose organic. But don’t buy if it’s not
certified.”
Reading Skills )
Extract B: Gambling with dirt: The odds for farmers is getting longer
Farming has always involved considerable risk, likened to a “gamble with dirt,” but climate
change is amplifying unpredictability in weather patterns and intensifying those risks. In
earlier decades, farmers could generally count on consistent harvest periods in late
November to early December, allowing for reliable planning and pricing.
Today, rising temperatures and erratic rainfall have shifted crop cycles, causing some
crops to ripen earlier yet then face heavy downpours or prolonged wet spells that harm
quality. Although overall annual rainfall totals may remain near average, its distribution has
become more uneven—sometimes triggering droughts followed by floods—complicating
decision-making on planting and harvesting. For instance, despite an El Nifio declaration
in 2023 that would typically imply drier conditions, parts of Australia experienced both
me
severe drought and flooding in the same season. Such extremes exacerbate the “fodder |
drought” in regions where livestock feed becomes scarce, forcing difficult choices like
livestock sales or even culling.
Rising input costs—for fertilisers, chemicals, fuel, and machinery maintenance—
compound the challenge, as farmers must invest more to safeguard yields under volatile
conditions. Much of Australia’s farmland is dedicated to grazing rather than cropping,
meaning the pressure to meet global protein demand remains high even when pasture
growth is threatened by weather swings. Farmers are exploring adaptations such as
altered sowing dates, drought-resistant varieties, diversified enterprises, and on-farm
water management systems to mitigate risks. Government and industry bodies also
emphasise the need for coordinated research into climate-resilient practices and policy
frameworks that support sustainable agriculture.
Despite mounting uncertainties, farmers continue to demonstrate resilience by investing in
new approaches, from precision agriculture technologies to regenerative soil techniques,
underscoring their determination to persist amid changing conditions. Community
awareness and supportive policy measures—such as improved drought relief programs
and incentives for sustainable practices—are vital to help farming remain viable in the long
term.

Extract A: Sea Safety - Letter to the editor
Once again another sea rescue that was completely unnecessary has taken place. Small
craft, sailing vessels and helicopters have been involved in a four-day search of our
coastline, often in appalling weather and dangerous seas because of human stupidity.
| am very pleased that the Haslan family was finally rescued from the serious danger they
were in, but the danger was of their own making. Reports indicate that the minimum safety
requirement and safety kits were not on board. Not to have the correct safety equipment,
sufficient safety floatation devices and communicating equipment and setting off past
Barr's Point into the open sea, can only be described as almost criminal negligence.
The weather forecast on the morning the family set out indicated rising seas and steadily
increasing winds, though only freshening during the afternoon to 17 - 21 knots. The area
outside Barr's Point is well known as a place where the current can run in the opposite
direction to the waves. When this happens the waves can overrun each other and this in
turn generates steep and dangerous rogue waves. In this part of the world, the weather
forecasts for fishermen and the general conditions north and south of Eastview are well
known, widely advertised and most people take the necessary precautions to ensure the
safety of the lives of their family.
What did this rescue cost in terms of official police, rescue personnel and volunteers? A
large sum of money no doubt. It is time people who, through their own ignorance, lack of
responsibility and common sense, were made to pay to our local council at least part of the
overall cost of their rescue.
Extract B: Excerpt from ‘The Coral Island: A Tale of the Pacific Ocean’ by R.M.
Ballantyne
| shall say little about the first part of our voyage. We had the usual amount of rough
weather and calm; also we saw many strange fish rolling in the sea, and | was greatly
delighted one day by seeing a shoal of flying fish dart out of the water and skim through
the air about a foot above the surface. They were pursued by dolphins, which feed on
them, and one flying-fish in its terror flew over the ship, struck on the rigging, and fell upon
the deck. Its wings were just fins elongated, and we found that they could never fly far at a
time, and never mounted into the air like birds, but skimmed along the surface of the sea.
Jack and | had it for dinner, and found it remarkably good.
When we approached Cape Horn, at the southern extremity of America, the weather
became very cold and stormy, and the sailors began to tell stories about the furious gales
and the dangers of that terrible cape. Each story outdid the one before in conjuring fearful
possibilities.
Nevertheless, we passed the dreaded cape without much rough weather, and, in the
course of a few weeks afterwards, were sailing gently, before a warm tropical breeze, over
the Pacific Ocean. Thus we proceeded on our voyage, sometimes bounding merrily before
a fair breeze, at other times floating calmly on the glassy wave and fishing for the curious
inhabitants of the deep - all of which, although the sailors thought little of them, were
strange, and interesting, and very wonderful to me.

The Teams
Henry Lawson
A cloud of dust on the long, white road,
And the teams go creeping on
Inch by inch with the weary load;
And by the power of the green-hide goad
The distant goal is won.
With eyes half-shut to the blinding dust,
And necks to the yokes bent low,
The bests are pulling as bullocks must;
And the shining tires might almost rust
While the spokes are turning slow.
With face half-hid by a broad-brimmed hat,
That shades from the heat's white waves,
And shouldered whip, with its green-hide plait,
The driver plots with a gait like that
Of his weary, patient slaves.
He wipes his brow, for the day is hot,
And spits to the left with spite;
He shouts at Bally, and flicks at Scot,
And raises dust from the back of Spot,
And spits to the dusty right.
He'll sometimes pause as a thing of form
In front of a settler's door
And ask for a drink, and remark "It's warm,"
Or say "There's signs of a thunderstorm";
But he seldom utters more

Hating Alison Ashley (PG)
Directed by Geoff Bennett
Screenplay by Christine Madafferi from the novel by Robin Klein
Rated PG
Cinemas Everywhere
Review by Sandra Hall
it's a girls’ world in this comic and colourful adaptation of a-much-loved children's
novel.
It should come as no surprise that Delta Goodrem doesn't convince as a 14-year-old
schoolgirl. Hiding under a Mona Lisa smile and a Goldilocks wig, she looks like a 20-year-
old pop star on the run from the paparazzi.
Not that it matters. The film of Hating Alison Ashley, Robin Klein's much-read children's
novel, has little to do with the real world. It's set in Ockerdom, a place where we patriotic
filmgoers have spent a lot of time lately, thanks to the run of comedies which have been
trying, with raucous relentlessness, to make themselves loveable in the happy-go-lucky
manner of The Castle.
Hating Alison Ashley is not really Alison's story. As Klein's many fans know, its narrator is
Alison's classmate, Erica Yurken (Saskia Burmeister), a talented self-dramatist, who
fancies she's been stranded in the wrong life. Her refined sensibilities, she thinks, are
more suited to some ivy-covered temple of learning than scungy, working-class Barringa
East, where she's been dumped among the delinquents of 9C. Whenever she can, she
escapes to the sick bay, where her impressive list of imaginary ailments has gained her a
reputation as a creative hypochondriac.
And life at home is no better. Although her sweet-natured mum (Tracy Mann) does her
best, Erica can't forgive her for taking up with Lennie (Richard Carter), a truck driver she
met at Parents Without Partners, or for giving her such unbearable siblings. Her chief
torturer is her elder sister, boy-mad Valjoy (Rachael Carpani), whose boots and big hair
are almost as scary as her interest in martial arts.
School improves for Erica with the arrival of Miss Belmont (Jean Kittson), whose fishnet
stockings and gallows humour give her the air of a semi-respectable dominatrix. Miss
Belmont does the previously unthinkable and keeps 9C in order. She also gives Erica high
marks and makes her fee! special - until the arrival of Goodrem's Alison Ashley.
Alison is perfection incarnate. For a minute or two, Erica fancies she has found a kindred
spirit. But Alison proves to be strangely aloof. And, even worse, the quality of her
classwork eclipses Erica's.

Claire Carmichael, Random House
People work out whether or not they want to read a novel by using all sorts of different
cues — the cover illustration, the blurb on the back, the length of the book and the size of

Extract A: Excerpt from ‘Brenda is the Night’ by Geoffrey McSkimming
In the great deserts of Egypt, where the hot and golden-grained sands stretch on and on
towards the shimmering, far away ends of the earth, miracles are said still to happen.
Everything out here is wide open and lonely. Nearly all of the desert land is dry, the sand
baked almost rock-hard in places by the sun. Sometimes, if you are travelling through this |
furnace of a place, you might come across an oasis — a small patch where there is a
water-hole, with palm trees and small plants called Lilies of the Nile growing around it.
Here you will find shade, and you will be able to fill your water-bottle and wet your
handkerchief and tie it around your neck to cool yourself. If you find an oasis in the desert,
you will be very lucky, as they are few and most definitely far between.
Not many people live in the desert. Those who do usually travel around a lot, not staying in
the one place for a very long time at all. Sometimes they will camp at an oasis for a few
weeks, but they will always move on, for they are usually fearful of meeting up with a
certain tribe — a tribe which has dwelt under the Egyptian sun for thousands of years. The
people who live out in the desert will do anything to avoid coming into contact with this
tribe (one man, long ago, was said to have glued ibis feathers to his body and a long
curved stick to his mouth, and then stood on one leg in the sand, crowing loudly, just so
the tribe would think he was a bird and maybe leave him alone), and so they keep
constantly on the move.
The reason why everyone avoids this particular tribe has nothing to do with dastardliness,
or with their being murderers or thieves or taxation cheats — because they’re not. Nor do
the tribe members make rude sounds or push people to the ground and sit on them,
actions which would automatically make them disagreeable. As a matter of fact, the tribe is
fairly harmless. As another matter of fact, they're not even human beings. They are, as
everybody who has journeyed through these wide sandy plains and hills knows, one of the
oldest wayfaring groups in all of the African continent: camels.
Extract B: What is a Mirage?
A mirage is an optical illusion. Most commonly observed in desert environments, mirages
arise when the sun-heated ground warms the adjacent layer of air more intensely than
the air above it, producing a steep temperature gradient. Since warmer air is less dense
than cooler air, light traversing these layers undergoes continual refraction—bending
gradually away from regions of lower density.
Travellers crossing arid expanses may glimpse what seems to be a shimmering oasis just
ahead—a patch of glimmering water fringed by palm trees and verdant foliage.
Compelled by thirst and hope, they advance, only to find the vision dissolving as they
approach. In reality, the water and trees lie far beyond the true horizon, their light
refracted upward by the denser, cooler air above the hot surface layer. This type of
mirage, known as an inferior mirage, produces inverted—or “upside-down’—images of
the distant scene directly beneath the upright image, explaining why one might perceive a
waterline or the glint of liquid on the desert floor.
Asimilar process occurs at sea under particular atmospheric conditions, giving rise to
superior mirages, in which cooler air lies closer to the ocean’s surface and warmer air sits
aloft. Light from a ship beyond the horizon can be bent downward into the colder layer,
causing the vessel to appear lifted, elongated or even inverted above its actual position—
sometimes floating eerily above the waterline. Mariners of old recorded such spectral
sightings, attributing them to supernatural forces, yet we now understand them as natural
consequences of atmospheric refraction.

Bushfire Weather
By Jeri Kroll
It’s cool in the hills,
breezes dart through houses like trapped birds
beating glass till they're free.
It’s clean up there. Smog doesn’t rain
Across the garden, smudging the birds of paradise,
fingerprinting the windowsills.
It’s calm in the hills when the frenzied heat
in the town bullies pedestrians.
The north wind eggs it on:
cotton wrapped like a second skin
loosens and billows, even sunglasses can’t screen the grit,
the earth in the driveway’s blown off,
vegetables wilt in the garden,
the city lies like an old dog.
In century heat, in the tinder-dry hills,
air has an edge, too, but shade is kinder.
Children swing across the Onkaparinga
into cool green slime. Cats pant under water tanks,
horse munch prickly grass under rattling trees.
By one o’clock the city has a compress on its head,
no longer looks at the hills
as if they meant afterlife.
The north-east wind dries sweat running down the spine,

Extract A: On the Darling River
The Darling - which is either a muddy gutter or a second Mississippi - is about six times as
long as the distance, in a straight line, from its head to its mouth. The state of the river is
vaguely, but generally understood to depend on some distant and foreign phenomena, to
which bushmen refer in an offhand tone of voice as "the Queenslan' rains", which seem to
be held responsible, in a general way, for most of the outback trouble.
It takes less than a year to go upstream by boat to Walgett or Bourke in a dry season
because the river is then a string of waterholes. After a while the passengers get sick of
climbing out of the boat while it is carried to the next long waterhole. They get sick of being
stuck in the same sort of place, in the same old way; they grow weary of seeing the same
old timer drop his swag on the bank opposite whenever the boat ties up for wood; they get
tired of lending him tobacco, and listening to his ideas, which are limited in number and
narrow in conception.
It shortens the journey to get out and walk; but then you will have to wait so long for your
luggage - unless you hump it with you.
We heard of a man who determined to stick to a Darling boat and travel the whole length
of the river. He was a newspaper man. He started on his voyage of discovery one Easter in
flood-time, and a month later the captain got bushed between the Darling and the South
Australian border. The water went away before he could find the river again, and he left his
boat in a scrub. They had a cargo of rations, and the crew stuck to the craft while the
tucker lasted; when it gave out they rolled up their swags and went to look for a station, but
didn't find one. The captain would study his watch and the sun, rig up dials and make out
courses, and follow them without success. They ran short of water, and didn't smell any for
weeks; they suffered terrible privations, and lost three of their number, not including the
newspaper man. There were even dark hints of considering the drawing of lots in
connection with something too terrible to mention. They crossed a thirty-mile plain at last,
and sighted a young Aboriginal girl. She led them to a boundary-rider's hut where they
were taken in and provided with rations.
Later on a syndicate was formed to explore the country and recover the boat; but they
found her thirty miles from the river and about eighteen from the nearest waterhole deep
enough to float her so they left her there.
Extract B: The Darling River Run
The Darling River Run is one of Australia’s most celebrated outback self-drive adventures,
tracing the course of the Darling River through western New South Wales. Depending on
where you begin—Walgett or Brewarrina—the journey covers roughly 730 km, though
extensions and detours (for example, starting upriver at Brewarrina or including side trips
to sites like White Cliffs) can stretch the itinerary to around 950 km in total. Most travellers
allow between ten days and two weeks to savour the full experience, though shorter or
longer road-trip variations are common.
Starting in the north at Walgett, drivers follow the Barwon River south to its junction with
the Darling at Bourke. From Bourke, the road clings to the riverbank, winding through the
tiny settlements of Louth and Tilpa, then beyond Wilcannia and Menindee—before finally
reaching Wentworth, where the Darling merges with the Murray River at the Victoria-New
South Wales border. Along this route, bitumen alternates with well-graded dirt tracks; after
rain, certain stretches can become impassable without a four-wheel-drive vehicle.
At every turn, the Darling River Run reveals layers of history and culture. In Brewarrina,
just south of Walgett, you can explore the ancient Aboriginal fish traps on the Barwon
stone weirs and pools, believed to be among the oldest human-made structures. Bourke
itself embodies “back o’ Bourke” outback character, with its river-front museums and walk-
through exhibits that chart colonial exploration and pastoral life. Further downstream,
historic pubs in Tilpa and the art-lined streets of Wilcannia speak to both hardship and
resilience in the remote bush.
The road skirts five national parks—Gundabooka, Toorale, Paroo-Darling, Kinchega and
Mungo—each offering its own spectacle of red dunes, coolabah woodlands and, at Mungo,
ancient lunette formations etched with millennia-old Indigenous footprints. Menindee
Lakes provide opportunities for birdwatching, canoeing and camping beside serene
floodplain lagoons. Thermal springs, river red gums and sweeping floodplains reveal the
Darling’s changing moods, from dusty drought to sudden inundation.
Practical planning is essential. A high-clearance 4WD is strongly recommended—not only
for unsealed road sections but also to ensure safe passage when river levels rise. Fuel,
water and supplies can be scarce: town-based fuel stations are found in Walgett,
Brewarrina, Bourke, Wilcannia, Menindee and Wentworth, but it’s wise to carry extra jerry
cans and drinking water. Mobile reception is intermittent; travellers should equip
themselves with a satellite phone or emergency beacon (EPIRB), plus spare tyres and
basic recovery gear. Before setting out, check in at local Visitor Information Centres for the
latest road-condition updates and insider tips

Do you Believe that a Child can Die
in the Middle of the Pacific Ocean?
By YEN-HA CHAU
Do you believe that a child can die
in the middle of the Pacific Ocean?
His boat in the middle of the ocean
the whole ocean surrounding him
while we have a soft drink
coffee or beer.
We say this coffee is too sweet
it’s not very good for our health
but he hasn't got a cup of sweet coffee even a drop of water.
His mother’s tears can’t save him.
He looks like a dried tomato.
He holds his little hands tightly.
He dies with his eyes open.
God can't even save him.
Nobody can save him.
You can hear
The sea wave's cry and the wind call his name.
You can see
Hell waving to him.
He is dying
Without a drop of water.
He is dead
in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.

The following is an interview conducted by Elizabeth Halley
Elizabeth Halley: What do you do on radio?
Paul Murphy: | am a presenter of a current affairs program called ‘PM’. ‘PM’ provides
an analysis of what is happening in Australia and the rest of the world.
EH: What do you do as a presenter of current affairs?
PM: You give introductions to reports and conduct comments on interviews. | imagine
that 35 percent and sometimes 70 percent of the program is me doing interviews.
You’re a presenter that is reliable. Your audience might only listen to you once or
twice a week but they know you are there.
EH: Can somebody else stand in for you if you are sick?
PM: | make a point of never being sick! I’ve always been there and that’s the way you
can build up an audience. | was a Canberra correspondent in 1969. | can ring
people like the Treasurer personally and ask a favour because I’ve been around
as long as he has. In this way the program can include famous or sought-after
personalities.
EH: So there are important people you know and can contact, and that makes you
very valuable to ‘PM’?
PM: | think that’s how the employers see it. It’s just familiarity — I’ve been a part of
journalism both here and overseas, and in television, so a lot of people know me.
EH: What sort of contact do you have with your audience ~— do they ring up?
PM: People contact us for a variety of reasons. Perhaps two percent of every
communication you get is thanking you for something. Mainly, it's annoyance,
saying, ‘You should know more about the story, are you aware that...?’ It’s all part
of the information gathering process. Often you feel you want to cut yourself off,
but that’s death professionally. You can’t — you have got to know what people
think and feel, even if you profoundly disagree with them.

sections.passage:
ARY THUER
On 3 May 1978, Gary Thuerk (USA) sent the first ‘spam’ (an unsolicited e-mail,
usually advertising a product or service) via ARPAnet, a system seen as the
predecessor to the internet.
Why exactly did you send your first spam e-mail?
| wanted to reach people in western USA to tell them about our mainframe-class server.
How many people were on your mailing List?
Over 400, which was about 25% of everyone online in the world at that time. We took the
names from a printed phone book and typed them in!
What do think of spam today?
| don’t get a lot of spam because | don’t leave my contact details on the Internet — chat
room, etc. Also, when people forward jokes to friends, they leave the e-mail list in there
and spammers can eventually get hold of it.
Does anybody ever blame you for the current volumes of spam today?
Oh yes — | get people who blame me but if | talk to them we normally end up smiling or
laughing about it.
Do you feel guilty?
No. of course not. If you take a plane flight and the airline loses your luggage, you don’t
blame the Wright brothers!
Why exactly are unsolicited e-mails called ‘spam’?
It came from a Monty Python’s Flying Circus sketch. Somebody who just watched it was
going through his unsolicited e-mails and complained that he was being spammed — and
everyone around him began singing the Monty Python spam song!
